speaker: Edwin
content: We're thinking about ten days in Japan in November. Two of us, first time there, not a huge budget. Where should we actually go and how do we get around?

speaker: Claude
content:
For a first trip, ten days, two people, not much budget — the classic Tokyo → Kyoto/Osaka corridor is genuinely the right answer. It's the one time "do the obvious thing" is correct: the transport is dense, English signage is everywhere, and you never backtrack.

## The route

**Tokyo — 4 nights.** Base in one place the whole time. Ueno, Asakusa, or Shinjuku for cheap-and-connected. Mix neighborhoods (Shibuya/Shimokitazawa, Yanaka, Tsukiji outer market) with one big day trip.

**Day trip from Tokyo — pick one:** Nikko (shrines + early-November foliage, peaks there ~first week of Nov) or Kamakura (temples + coast, cheaper and closer). Hakone is the third option but works better as a stopover than a day trip.

**Hakone — 1 night, optional.** Onsen ryokan, Mt Fuji views if the weather cooperates. It sits between Tokyo and Kyoto so it costs you almost nothing in transit. Cheapest way to get a ryokan night without a detour.

**Kyoto — 4 nights.** Late November is peak foliage — spectacular and genuinely mobbed. Temples open at 8–9am and the difference between 8:30 and 11:00 at Fushimi Inari or Arashiyama is night and day.

**Osaka — 1 night at the end,** or just day-trip it from Kyoto (28 min, ~¥580). Nara is a better day trip than Osaka if you only get one. Himeji Castle if you want a third.

Fly into Tokyo (Haneda > Narita) and out of Osaka Kansai — "open-jaw" tickets usually cost the same as a round trip and save you a wasted travel day.

## Getting around

**Skip the national JR Pass.** It went to ¥50,000/person for 7 days in late 2023 and no longer pays for itself on this route. Tokyo→Kyoto is ~¥14,000 and Kyoto→Osaka is pocket change; you'd need to be doing a lot more long-distance riding to break even. Just buy point-to-point.

**Get IC cards** (Suica/Pasmo in Tokyo, ICOCA in Kansai — all interchangeable). Tap for every subway, bus, train, and convenience store. If you have an iPhone, add Suica directly to Apple Wallet and top up with a card — that sidesteps the physical-card supply issues entirely and is the single best quality-of-life move.

**Shinkansen:** book via the SmartEX app or just buy at the station. Non-reserved cars are cheaper and fine outside holidays. Get a reserved seat on the Tokyo→Kyoto leg though, especially on a weekend in foliage season.

**Cheaper alternatives if the budget is tight:** overnight highway buses (Willer, ~¥5,000 Tokyo→Kyoto, saves a hotel night but costs you a rough sleep), or budget flights on Peach/Jetstar which can undercut the Shinkansen but add airport transit time.

**Worth buying regionally:** a Hakone Free Pass if you go there, and the Kansai-area day passes for Kyoto/Nara/Osaka. These are small and actually pay off, unlike the big one.

## Rough budget

Per person, excluding international flights, at roughly ¥150 to the dollar:

- Lodging: ¥7,000–9,000/night for a business hotel double (APA, Toyoko Inn, Sotetsu Fresa) — so ~¥40,000 each for the trip
- Intercity transport: ~¥20,000–25,000
- Food: ¥3,000–5,000/day eating well at conveyor sushi, ramen shops, department-store food halls, and konbini
- Entry fees: ¥500–1,000 per temple, adds up faster than you'd think

Call it **¥110,000–140,000 (~$750–950) each on the ground.** The ryokan night, if you do one, is ¥15,000–25,000 per person on its own — worth it once.

## Book now, not later

Late-November Kyoto hotels sell out and prices roughly double. If your dates land in the second half of the month, lock lodging in well ahead; everything else can wait.

Two things that would change my advice: are your dates early or late November (that flips the foliage from Nikko/Tokyo to Kyoto), and do you want a rural/onsen night in the mix or would you rather stay in cities the whole time? Tell me and I'll turn this into an actual day-by-day.

content:
Looked it up — and the answer has a wrinkle I didn't know about, because prices split into two tiers as of last October.

## Current 7-day Ordinary pass

| Where you buy | Price |
|---|---|
| Official JR Pass website | **¥50,000** |
| Overseas travel agents | **¥53,000** |

Full ladder: 14-day is ¥80,000 online / ¥84,000 agency, 21-day ¥100,000 / ¥105,000. Green Car 7-day is ¥70,000 / ¥74,000.

JR raised prices ~5–6% on **October 1, 2026** — but the increase only hit overseas sales agents. The official online reservation site held its old prices, and the end date for that "will be announced once decided." So there's no deadline to plan around, just an open-ended window that could close. If you buy, buy direct.

## Does it pay off for your trip?

No, and not close. Here's the actual arithmetic for Tokyo → Kyoto → Osaka:

- Tokyo→Kyoto, Hikari reserved: **¥13,850** (¥13,320 unreserved; ¥14,250 in super-peak season)
- Kyoto→Osaka: ~¥580
- Kyoto→Nara: ~¥720
- Osaka→Kansai Airport on the Haruka: ~¥2,400
- Tokyo local JR lines across four days: maybe ¥1,500

That's roughly **¥19,000–25,000** of JR-eligible travel. The pass is ¥50,000. You'd be paying double for the privilege.

Two things make it worse for this route specifically. The pass doesn't cover the Nozomi — the fast Tokyo–Kyoto service — without a surcharge, so you're on the slower Hikari. And the good Nikko route is Tobu, a private railway the pass doesn't touch at all.

To break even you'd need to bolt on something like a Tokyo–Hiroshima round trip, which is a different, more rushed vacation than the one I'd recommend for a first visit.

So: point-to-point tickets, IC card for everything local, and put the ¥25,000 you save toward the ryokan night.
